posts.title: The Bombmaker Next Door
posts.description: When John Nelson died in the summer of 2025, he left behind more than 400 explosive devices, a literal minefield that ran through his home in the suburbs between Manchester and Liverpool. (“Minefield” may be misleading; there were also secret pits filled with spikes.) The painstaking work of clearing Nelson’s home of explosives prompted “one of the largest domestic evacuations of its kind in recent British history,” writes Andrew Kersley, who spent months interviewing the experts who kept Nelson’s home from exploding, as well as the neighbors who seemingly loved him. “I guess it was just his pastime,” one tells Kersley. Indeed! During a second search after Nelson’s death, police had discovered a small tobacco tin containing explosives, with wires protruding from it. RY set up his X-ray machine and stepped into the adjoining room while it scanned the tin. posts.title: Nothing but Highlights: Is Power Slap the Sport We Deserve?
posts.description: Slapping someone in the face is now a sport. Yes, I’m surprised too. But in an era of ever-shrinking attention spans, getting to the point (or the slap) within seconds seems to be the surest way to hold viewers. According to its founder, Dana White, “Power Slap has secured more sponsorship revenue in its first two years than UFC did in its first decade.” Stuart McGurk deftly guides us through the rise of the slap, and talks with those who fear the consequences of hitting someone round the head as hard as you can. The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. posts.title: Vegetabilities: A Harvest of a Reading List on Vegetables
posts.description: Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times. Longreads has published hundreds of original stories—personal essays, reported features, reading lists, and more—and more than 14,000 editor’s picks. And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today. I want to support Longreads Whenever I clean spinach or other greens, I get a curious feeling. I see a post-apocalyptic future, where a white-haired version of me is cleaning greens amid the ruins, salvaging every tiny, edible leaf. I then imagine my ancestors doing the same thing a hundred thousand years ago. Nothing heroic about this work, no high drama, no awesome mammoth-hunting. Just the fundamental stuff that keeps life going. “In the temperate and tropical regions where it appears that hominids evolved into human beings, the principal food of the species was vegetable,” Ursula K.
